content:
The Mothman story has always been something of a cross between Appalachian folklore and a campfire myth. But the place associated with many of the Mothman sightings near Point Pleasant has a very real industrial footprint.

Along the Ohio River, the West Virginia Ordnance Works was built during World War II to manufacture TNT -- and abandoned three years later as the need diminished. The process was dependent on corrosive acids and known for generating massive volumes of toxic waste. When a facility like that shuts down, the chemistry doesn't simply disappear. Lagoons, byproducts, and buried waste can persist for decades, slowly migrating through soil and groundwater. "Reclaimed" land, in many cases -- especially here, where parts of the former works are now designated as a wildlife refuge and campground -- is simply land where the surface has been quieted, not cured.

So, when people report strange lights, chemical smells, headaches, anxiety, or even the sense that the woods feel wrong, it's worth asking whether the environment is shaping perception long before any formal testing confirms contamination.

That context reframes the first Mothman sightings in 1966 around the old TNT area.

Industrial landscapes can prime the nervous system. Isolation, darkness, chronic stress, and low-level chemical exposure all influence how humans process sensory information and perceive threat. Not everyone will experience overt symptoms, but communities often register patterns collectively -- especially when the land itself offers visible warnings: discolored ponds, unnatural stillness, or dead zones where nothing grows right.

Once a few witnesses describe glowing red eyes and a fast-moving shape, expectation begins to do its work. People scan the tree line differently. Ambiguity narrows. The "creature" becomes a shared language for something that feels real but resists explanation.

Then, in 1967 -- a year after the first Mothman sighting -- the Silver Bridge collapsed killing 46 people and the story hardened into something else entirely.

Humans are pattern-making machines. Randomness is difficult to live with, especially in the wake of public tragedy. What begins as folklore shifts into a deeper, more unsettling question: what was actually in those woods?

Residual TNT compounds, acid waste, and industrial byproducts can persist in the environment, creating long-term exposure pathways without consent or awareness. When regulation and measurement lag behind reality, communities reach for other narratives because they are trying to interpret real signals with the tools available.

This is one theory of many that might explain the Mothman. But it is a theory worth considering because the same pattern is playing out again -- just as it did with our communities' discoveries of C8. The industrial solvent is one of many forever chemicals or PFAS. They are invisible and persistent. They can be found in nearly every living organism, and nearly every body of water on Earth.

It took more than five decades to discover the odorless, colorless poison contaminating our local water supplies. It's something we might still know nothing about if not for the failure of an entire herd of cattle in West Virginia -- on the Tennant farm -- about twenty miles north of the TNT site.

Appalachians know this cycle well: confusion first, then dismissal. Symptoms that don't quite connect. Then, years later, science arrives -- slowly, and often too late.

That is where environmental justice enters the story.

Because the cost of uncertainty is not shared equally. It falls on real people -- not on the institutions that profited from wartime production or industrial expansion. "Not fully studied" and "not fully remediated" are not neutral phrases. They are risk statements -- especially when land use changes, construction begins, and buried waste is disturbed, mobilizing what was once contained.

The good news is that ordinary people are not powerless.

Industrial development leaves a paper trail long before it makes headlines. Permits are public, even if they are difficult to navigate. Public comment periods provide an opportunity -- one that agencies are required to enter into the record. FOIA requests can uncover internal communications, emails, and reports that never make it into public-facing summaries.

And, showing up matters. County meetings. Public hearings. Zoning discussions. Decisions get quieter when rooms are empty.

If the TNT site is ultimately buried beneath a data center, as proposed, we may never know whether the Mothman was an unknown biological anomaly, a misidentified presence, or something shaped -- at least in part -- by environmental exposure.

This chemical theory is one of many.

And, it is worth mentioning that not every unexplained sighting in the region fits neatly into this box. Ten days before the first Mothman sighting in November 1966, a sewing machine salesman reported an encounter of a different kind. This event took place roughly 20 miles in a different direction from the Tennant farm.

Since 1964, the region has seen numerous reports of UFO activity. Those reports continue to this day. And, a number of them are significant.

But that is a different story for another day.

If the Mothman is only a metaphor, this is the truth behind the legend: What gets buried doesn't stay buried. And, sometimes what rises from the depths is far more frightening than anything we could have imagined.

Callie J. Lyons is an investigative journalist and author whose work has explored environmental contamination, public health, and the stories of Appalachia. Her groundbreaking 2007 book, Stain-Resistant, Nonstick, Waterproof, and Lethal: The Hidden Dangers of C8 PFAS and Our Water, is now available in paperback for the first time on Amazon.
